title: Acute Sore Throat Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing acute sore throat, pharyngitis and tonsillitis; identifying airway-threatening and deep-neck complications, recognising important alternatives, and supporting proportionate treatment, referral and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Assess the acute sore throat rather than assuming tonsillitis from tonsillar appearance alone. Establish airway safety, illness severity, hydration, likely cause and whether complications or alternative diagnoses require a different pathway.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Airway compromise, supraglottitis or another cause of upper-airway obstruction.
Peritonsillar infection or abscess (quinsy).
Deep neck-space infection.
Severe systemic illness or sepsis.
Inability to swallow sufficient fluids or medication.
Uncomplicated acute pharyngitis or tonsillitis.
Important alternatives including infectious mononucleosis and scarlet fever.
Immunosuppression or another factor substantially increasing complication risk.
items.importantLimitation: Tonsillar erythema, enlargement and exudate do not reliably distinguish viral from bacterial infection. Interpret the overall clinical pattern rather than tonsillar appearance alone.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Define the pattern, severity and time course, then look for features that suggest a complication or alternative diagnosis.

items.title: Presenting illness
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset, duration and whether symptoms are improving, stable or worsening.
Unilateral or bilateral throat pain.
Fever, rigors or marked systemic upset.
Odynophagia and whether solids, liquids, medication and saliva can be swallowed.
Previous tonsillitis, quinsy or significant throat infection.
Recent assessment, antibiotics and clinical response.

items.title: Respiratory and viral features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Cough.
Coryza, rhinorrhoea or nasal congestion.
Hoarseness.
Other upper-respiratory symptoms.
Relevant household, school, workplace or other close-contact illness.

items.title: Features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
mustConfirmOrExclude: Marked fatigue with posterior or generalised lymphadenopathy — consider infectious mononucleosis.
Sandpaper-textured rash or strawberry tongue — consider scarlet fever.
Oral ulceration, candidiasis or another atypical mucosal lesion.
Persistent unilateral throat pain, referred otalgia, persistent tonsillar asymmetry, neck mass or unexplained weight loss.

items.title: Background risk
mustConfirmOrExclude: Immunosuppression or significant comorbidity.
Medicines associated with immunosuppression, neutropenia or agranulocytosis where relevant.
Known drug allergies and recent antimicrobial exposure.
Ability to obtain treatment and access reassessment.

sections.title: Red flags and complications
sections.intro: Positive or evolving features should change disposition. Do not manage these presentations as uncomplicated tonsillitis.

items.title: Airway compromise / supraglottitis
urgentFeatures: Stridor or respiratory distress.
Drooling or inability to manage secretions.
Rapidly progressive dysphagia.
Markedly altered or weak voice with significant illness.
Severe odynophagia with little obvious oropharyngeal abnormality.
Tripod positioning, cyanosis, exhaustion or altered consciousness.
implications: Possible upper-airway obstruction or supraglottitis; follow the appropriate emergency and ENT pathway.
items.importantLimitation: Do not repeatedly manipulate or aggressively examine the pharynx when significant supraglottic airway obstruction is suspected.

items.title: Quinsy / peritonsillar abscess
urgentFeatures: Severe unilateral throat pain.
Trismus.
Muffled 'hot potato' voice.
Drooling or substantial dysphagia.
Unilateral peri-tonsillar or soft-palate swelling, with or without uvular displacement.
implications: Suspected quinsy requires urgent same-day ENT or hospital assessment.
items.importantLimitation: Uvular displacement supports the diagnosis when present but is not required.

items.title: Deep neck-space infection
urgentFeatures: Severe throat or neck pain with neck swelling or stiffness.
Painful restriction of neck movement.
Trismus, drooling, dysphagia or muffled voice.
Stridor or toxic appearance.
Progression despite apparently appropriate treatment.
implications: Possible retropharyngeal, parapharyngeal or other deep neck-space infection; urgent specialist assessment is required.

items.title: Severe systemic illness
urgentFeatures: Physiological instability or markedly abnormal observations.
Altered mental state, poor peripheral perfusion or rapidly worsening systemic symptoms.
Clinical concern for sepsis.
implications: Follow the appropriate acute illness or sepsis pathway.

items.title: Unable to maintain hydration or oral treatment
urgentFeatures: Unable to swallow liquids or required medication.
Persistent vomiting or inability to retain fluids.
Markedly reduced urine output or clinical dehydration.
implications: Community oral treatment may be unsafe; reassess hydration and disposition.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examine the patient as a whole before concentrating on the tonsils. Establish physiological stability, airway safety, hydration and whether findings are symmetrical and uncomplicated.

items.title: General assessment and observations
howToTest: Assess overall appearance, distress and ability to communicate normally.
Observe respiratory effort, voice and whether the patient is managing secretions.
Record temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation where clinically indicated.
implications: Airway, swallowing or physiological abnormalities take priority over tonsillar findings or use of a sore-throat scoring tool.

items.title: Oral cavity and oropharynx
howToTest: Inspect the oral cavity and pharynx with adequate illumination.
Assess tonsillar size, symmetry, erythema and exudate.
Inspect the soft palate and peri-tonsillar tissues and assess uvular position.
Look for ulceration, vesicles, petechiae, candidiasis or another atypical mucosal appearance.
abnormal: Marked unilateral tonsillar or soft-palate swelling.
Extensive ulceration, necrosis or atypical membrane.
Significant asymmetry unexplained by an acute symmetrical infection.
implications: Unilateral peri-tonsillar findings increase concern for quinsy.
Atypical mucosal findings should prompt consideration of another diagnosis.

items.title: Neck and lymph nodes
howToTest: Inspect and palpate for cervical lymphadenopathy, unilateral swelling and tenderness.
Assess anterior and posterior cervical nodes where relevant.
Assess neck movement when deep infection is a concern.
normal: Mild tender cervical lymphadenopathy may accompany uncomplicated infection.
abnormal: Persistent or unexplained focal neck mass.
implications: Posterior or generalised lymphadenopathy may support infectious mononucleosis in the appropriate context.
Neck swelling or stiffness with severe throat symptoms raises concern for deep infection.

items.title: Hydration
howToTest: Assess oral intake, urine output and clinical hydration.
Assess peripheral perfusion and haemodynamic status where indicated.
normal: Drinking adequately with normal or near-normal urine output.
abnormal: Unable to drink, markedly reduced urine output or evidence of significant dehydration.
implications: Hydration status may determine disposition even when the throat infection itself appears uncomplicated.

sections.title: Clinical decision support
sections.intro: Use an existing sore-throat scoring tool after serious pathology and important alternative diagnoses have been considered.

items.title: Antimicrobial decision support
mustConfirmOrExclude: Use @feverpain or @centor-criteria where appropriate.
Interpret the result alongside illness severity, comorbidity and suitability for community management.
items.importantLimitation: These tools support antimicrobial decision-making; they do not diagnose bacterial infection and do not determine disposition in an acutely unwell patient.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses and investigations
sections.intro: Consider alternative diagnoses when the clinical pattern is atypical or the illness is not following the expected course.

items.title: Investigations
mustConfirmOrExclude: Routine investigations are not required for most uncomplicated acute sore throats.
Consider testing for infectious mononucleosis when the clinical picture is compatible and the result would change advice or management.
Do not routinely use throat swabs solely to decide whether an otherwise uncomplicated sore throat requires antibiotics unless a local or public-health pathway requires testing.
Consider blood tests where there is significant systemic illness, dehydration, immunosuppression, suspected complication or prolonged or atypical illness.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Management should reflect illness severity, likely benefit from antibiotics, ability to maintain hydration and treatment, and access to reassessment.

items.title: Uncomplicated acute sore throat
mustConfirmOrExclude: Explain that most uncomplicated acute sore throats improve within about 1 week.
Encourage adequate oral fluids.
Treat pain and fever appropriately.
Use @feverpain or @centor-criteria to guide antimicrobial strategy where appropriate.
Avoid antibiotics when expected benefit is low.
If using a back-up antibiotic, give clear instructions for when to start it.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: Airway is safe and the patient is physiologically stable.
No red-flag complication or serious alternative diagnosis is suspected.
Oral fluids and medication can be tolerated.
Pain can be managed adequately.
The patient or carer understands the plan and can access reassessment.

items.title: Escalate or refer
urgentFeatures: Any feature in the red flags and complications section.
Rapid or significant clinical deterioration.
Significant immunosuppression or comorbidity that makes community management unsafe.
implications: Use the appropriate emergency, ENT, acute medical or local referral pathway according to the suspected diagnosis and severity.

sections.title: Safety-netting
sections.intro: Give clear advice about expected recovery and when urgent reassessment is required.

items.title: Advise urgent reassessment if
safetyNetting: Swallowing deteriorates or the patient cannot swallow saliva or fluids.
Drooling, markedly altered voice or restricted mouth opening develops.
Throat pain becomes markedly unilateral or rapidly more severe.
The patient becomes systemically very unwell.
Symptoms worsen significantly or are not beginning to improve within about 1 week.

items.title: Back-up antibiotic advice
safetyNetting: Where a back-up antibiotic has been provided, give clear instructions about when to start it and when further assessment is required.
